unit.title: Provide basic manicure and pedicure service

summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, hygienic basic manicure and pedicure: consult the client and check the hands and feet for conditions that stop or change the service, prepare a clean station, remove polish, shape and file the nails, care for the cuticles, smooth hard skin, give a hand or foot massage, and apply polish neatly. You will also learn to handle nail products safely, care for the foot spa and tools, give aftercare advice and keep client records.

blocks.p: A basic manicure cleans, shapes and polishes the fingernails and cares for the skin of the hands. A basic pedicure does the same for the feet and toenails. They are among the most popular services in Jamaican salons and nail studios, and they are often the first service a new trainee gives to a paying client. They are also services in which infection passes easily from one client to the next if the tools, the water and the technician's hands are not clean.

This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. It covers the basic services with polish, the hygiene that makes them safe, and the judgement to recognise a nail or skin condition that needs a doctor rather than a nail technician.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks, a basic manicure with polish and a basic pedicure with foot spa care, each given to a partner in your group while the assessor watches. The assessor looks at your hygiene, your consultation and record card, your technique and your clean-up, not only the finished nails.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hands, feet and work area, never a client's face.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Nail services touch skin, nails, warm water and sometimes blood. Fungal nail infections, athlete's foot, warts and bacterial infections can all pass from client to client on tools, towels, files, water and hands. Most of what makes this unit safe is **hygiene**, and most of hygiene is habit.

head: Word
What it means
Used for
rows: Cleaning
Removing dirt, skin, dust and product with soap (detergent) and water and a brush. It always comes **first**: disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Every tool, bowl and surface, before it is disinfected.
Disinfecting
Using an approved chemical, mixed as its label says, to kill most germs on a cleaned tool or surface. The tool stays fully covered for the **contact time** on the label.
Metal tools, bowls, the foot spa, the station top.
Sterilising
Killing all germs, including spores. An **autoclave** does this with steam under pressure.
Metal tools, where the Centre has an autoclave and the maker says the tool can take it.
Antiseptic
A product that reduces germs on skin.
The client's hands or feet before the service; your hands.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet is for storing tools that are already clean and disinfected. It does not disinfect dirty tools. Clean metal tools are kept in a closed container, so that they stay clean until they are used.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Group
Examples
Rule
rows: Reusable metal tools
Cuticle pushers, cuticle nippers, toenail clippers, metal foot files
Clean, then disinfect or sterilise, after every client. Store closed.
Single-use items
Emery boards (paper files), orange sticks, cotton wool, toe separators, foam buffers, wooden spatulas, pumice stones where the Centre's rules say
Used on one client only, then thrown away or given to the client. A porous item such as an emery board cannot be disinfected.
Sharps
Any blade, broken glass, a used lancet
Straight into the **sharps box**: a closed, puncture-proof container, never the ordinary bin.

ul: Wash your hands with soap and water **before and after every client**, to stop germs passing between clients and yourself. Dry them on a clean towel or paper.
Keep your own nails short, clean and free of rough edges, and wear no rings or bracelets that trap dirt or scratch the client.
Cleanse the client's hands or feet with soap and water, or an antiseptic wipe or spray, before you begin.
Wear disposable gloves where there is a risk of touching blood or broken skin, when cleaning the foot spa, and when the Centre's rules say so.
Cover any cut on your own hands with a waterproof plaster.

blocks.h: Towels, water and the foot spa

ul: A **fresh towel for every client**, for the hands and again for the feet. A towel used on a client's feet goes straight into the laundry and is washed hot. Never dry a face or hands with a foot towel.
Fresh water in the finger bowl and the foot spa for every client, at a comfortable temperature, tested with your inner wrist or elbow.

After each pedicure the **foot spa or pedicure bowl is drained, cleaned and disinfected as the maker's instructions say**, including the jets if it is a whirlpool spa. Bacteria breed in warm water left in a spa.
Wipe the station top, the arm rest and the chair with disinfectant between clients.

head: Manicure station
Pedicure station
rows: Clean table with good light; a clean towel and a cushion or folded towel for the client's arm
A comfortable chair for the client with her feet supported on a rest; a low stool for you
Finger bowl of warm, soapy water
Foot spa or bowl, clean and disinfected, with warm water and foot soak
Disinfected pusher and nippers in a closed container
Disinfected toenail clippers, pusher and nippers in a closed container
New emery board, orange sticks, cotton wool
New file, orange sticks, toe separators, pumice stone or foot file
Polish remover, cuticle softener, hand cream, base coat, colours, top coat
Polish remover, cuticle softener, foot cream, base coat, colours, top coat
Lined, covered bin; sharps box; record card; disinfectant spray
Lined, covered bin; sharps box; record card; gloves; dry towels for the floor

blocks.note: Set everything out **before** the client sits down, in the order you will use it. Hunting for the nippers with a client's wet hand in yours looks unprofessional and wastes her time.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The nail, the skin and conditions you may find

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters
rows: Nail plate
The hard, see-through part of the nail that you file and polish.
It must be clean and oil-free for polish to stick.
Free edge
The part of the nail plate that grows past the fingertip or toe.
The part you shape and file.
Nail bed
The skin under the nail plate; it gives the nail its pink colour.
Filing too deep or pressing hard hurts it.
Matrix
The living part under the skin at the base of the nail, where new nail cells are made. The pale half-moon (lunula) is the part you can see.
Pressing hard here can damage the new nail.
Cuticle
The thin layer of dead skin that sticks to the nail plate near its base.
It is softened and gently pushed back; it is not cut.
Nail walls and grooves
The skin at the sides of the nail.
Do not dig into the grooves: it causes ingrown nails.

ul: A fingernail takes about **four to six months** to grow from base to tip; toenails grow more slowly and take about a year or more.
**Leuconychia** is the name for small white spots on the nail plate. They usually come from a small knock to the matrix, grow out with the nail and are harmless: the service can go ahead.
A **hangnail** is a small piece of torn skin at the side of a nail. It is trimmed with the nippers.
A **callus** is a thick, hard patch of skin that forms on the heel or sole from pressure and rubbing. Some hard skin protects the foot; too much cracks and hurts.

blocks.p: The consultation finds out what the client wants and checks that her hands or feet are safe to treat. Do it with the client seated comfortably, in good light, after you have washed your hands.

head: Ask about
Why
rows: What she wants: shape, length, colour; manicure, pedicure or both
Sets the service and the price.
What she does with her hands each day: work, hobbies, sport
A cashier, a cook or a nurse needs short, strong nails; long oval nails suit someone whose work is light. This question, more than any other, decides the shape and length.
Health: diabetes, poor circulation, recent injury, pregnancy
A client with diabetes needs extra care. Swelling or a recent injury may stop the service.
Allergies and past reactions, for example to polish, remover, nickel or latex
So you can avoid the product or the glove.
Medicines
Some make the skin thin, bruise easily or bleed longer.
Nail problems: splitting, biting, fungal infection in the past
Guides your advice and the care you take.

blocks.p: Then **look** closely at the nails and the skin, back and front, and between the toes for a pedicure. Explain what you plan, agree it and the price, and write it on the record card.

A **contraindication** is a condition or reason that means a treatment must not be carried out, or must be changed. Infections stop the service: they can spread to you, to your tools and to the next client. Other conditions mean you adapt, or avoid an area.

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Paronychia (an infection of the skin around a nail)
Red, swollen, painful skin at the side or base of the nail, sometimes with pus.
**Do not treat** that hand or foot. Refer to a doctor.
Fungal nail infection
Thick, yellow or brown, crumbly nails that may lift from the nail bed.
**Do not treat** those nails. Advise the client to see a doctor or pharmacist. Fungi spread on files and clippers.
Athlete's foot (tinea pedis)
Itchy, red, peeling or cracked skin, often between the toes; may smell.
**Do not give the pedicure.** Refer to a pharmacist or doctor. It is a fungal infection and spreads easily in a foot spa.
Warts and verrucae
Small, rough, raised growths on the hands; on the feet, flat, hard spots with black dots that hurt when pressed.
**Do not touch or treat** the area. Warts are caused by a virus and spread. Refer.
Open cuts, grazes, sores or bleeding
Broken skin.
Avoid the area; if it is large or infected, do not treat. Refer.
Swelling, bruising, a sprain or a recent fracture
A swollen, discoloured or painful hand or foot.
Do not treat until it has healed. Refer if it is unexplained.
Severe eczema or psoriasis
Red, cracked, bleeding or weeping skin.
Do not treat broken skin. Mild, unbroken dry patches: carry on gently with mild products.
A nail lifting away from its bed, or badly damaged
A white or yellow area where the nail has separated.
Do not file or push there; refer.
Ingrown toenail
The nail edge growing into the skin; red and sore.
Avoid the area; refer to a doctor or podiatrist. Do not dig the nail out.
Diabetes
Nothing to see at first; ask.
Carry on **with extra care** (see below), or ask for a doctor's advice first.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not tell the client what she has. Say kindly and in private what you have seen, explain that you cannot treat the area today for her own safety, and suggest a doctor or pharmacist. Write it on the record card. Afterwards, clean and disinfect everything she touched.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Diabetes can reduce the feeling in the feet and slow the blood flow to them. The client may not feel water that is too hot, too much pressure, or a small cut, and **small cuts on the feet may heal slowly and become badly infected**. So:

ul: Ask at the consultation, and ask her to check with her doctor before a pedicure if she is unsure.
Look carefully for cuts, sores, colour changes and swelling. If you find any, do not treat the area; refer her.
Test the water temperature carefully and keep the soak short.
Do not cut the cuticles or use sharp tools close to the skin. Cut the nails straight across and file gently.
Smooth hard skin only lightly; never use a blade.
Use gentle massage pressure.
Advise her to check her feet every day and to wear shoes that fit well.
Record everything.

sections.title: Tools, products and their safe use

head: Tool
What it is for
Care
rows: Emery board (nail file)
Shaping and smoothing the free edge of natural nails. The finer side finishes the edge.
Single-use: throw it away or give it to the client.
Orange stick (orangewood stick)
Wrapped in cotton wool, it pushes back softened cuticle and cleans under the free edge; dipped in remover, it tidies polish off the skin.
Single-use.
Cuticle pusher (metal or rubber-tipped)
Gently pushing back softened cuticle.
Reusable: clean, then disinfect or sterilise.
Cuticle nippers
Trimming **hangnails and loose dead skin only**. Never for cutting the living cuticle or the skin.
Reusable: clean, then disinfect or sterilise. Keep the tips closed when not in use.
Toenail clippers
Cutting toenails straight across.
Reusable: clean, then disinfect or sterilise.
Pumice stone or foot file
Smoothing hard skin on the heels and soles.
Pumice is porous: single-use or the client's own, as the Centre's rules say. A metal foot file is cleaned and disinfected.
Finger bowl
Soaking the fingers in warm, soapy water.
Washed and disinfected; fresh water each client.
Foot spa or pedicure bowl
Soaking the feet.
Drained, cleaned and disinfected after every client, as the maker says.
Toe separators
Keeping the toes apart while polish is applied and dries.
Single-use.
Buffer
Smoothing ridges and giving a natural shine.
Foam buffers are single-use.
Spatula
Taking cream from a tub without putting fingers in it.
Single-use, or cleaned and disinfected.

head: Product
What it does
Take care
rows: Nail polish remover (acetone or non-acetone)
Dissolves old polish.
Flammable; strong fumes; dries the skin and nail. Non-acetone is gentler but slower.
Cuticle softener or remover
Softens dead cuticle skin so it can be eased off the nail plate.
Leave it on only for the time the maker says, then push back and wash it off; it can irritate skin if left on.
Hand cream or massage cream; foot cream
Softens the skin and gives slip for the massage.
Must be removed from the nail plate before polish.
Foot soak
Cleans and softens the feet in the spa water.
Use the amount the maker says.
Base coat
A clear coat that protects the nail from staining and helps the colour stick.
Thin.
Coloured polish
The colour.
Two thin coats.
Top coat
A clear coat put on last to protect the colour and add shine.
Seals the free edge.
Cuticle oil
Conditions the cuticle skin.
Applied at the end and for home care.
Paraffin wax (optional treatment)
Warm wax that softens dry hands and feet.
Test the wax on the inside of your own wrist before it touches the client.

ul: Nail polish, remover and many cleansers are **flammable**: keep them away from heat, flames, cigarettes and sunlight.
They give off **fumes**. Work in a well-ventilated room so the fumes are carried away, keep lids closed when bottles are not in use, and keep only the amount you need at the station.
Keep every product in its own labelled container. Never pour remover into an unlabelled or drink bottle.
Read the label and the safety data sheet, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
Wipe up spills at once. Put used cotton pads into a lined, covered bin so the fumes do not fill the room.
Store products in a cool, dry place, lids tight, out of the reach of children.

blocks.note: If polish remover or any product splashes into an eye, rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean, cool water for several minutes and get help. If a product irritates the skin, wash it off with water, stop the service and record the reaction.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: An electric foot spa is water and electricity together. Check the plug and cable before use, keep the socket and cable away from spilled water, use it with dry hands, and never fill or empty it while it is plugged in unless the maker says you may. Jamaica's supply is 110 V, or 220 V for some equipment, at 50 Hz: check the label on the spa matches the socket. Wipe up water on the floor at once so nobody slips.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The client sits facing you across the table, her forearm resting on a cushion or folded towel so her arm and shoulder are relaxed. You sit with a straight back and the work in good light.

flow: Consult, check the hands and fill in the record card
Wash your hands; cleanse the client's hands
Remove old polish
Check the nails again
Shape and file
Soak one hand in the finger bowl
Apply cuticle softener; push back the cuticles; nip hangnails only
Clean under the free edge
Repeat for the other hand
Hand and arm massage
Remove cream and oil from the nail plates
Base coat, two thin coats of colour, top coat
Tidy any polish off the skin
Check the finish; give aftercare advice
Clean up and complete the record

ul: Old polish comes off **first**, so that you can see the nails and the skin and check for problems that the colour was hiding.

Soak a cotton pad with remover, **press it on the nail for a moment** so the polish softens, then **wipe from the cuticle towards the tip** in one movement. Pressing and wiping outwards stops dark polish from being smeared into the skin.
Use a fresh pad for each hand, and a wrapped orange stick dipped in remover for polish caught in the corners.
Keep the remover away from the skin as much as you can: it dries it.

head: Shape
What it looks like
Suits
rows: Square
Straight sides and a straight free edge with sharp corners.
Strong nails; a modern look. The corners can catch and snag.
Squoval (square-oval)
A straight edge with softened, rounded corners.
Most clients: strong and practical, with no sharp corners.
Round
Follows the curve of the fingertip.
Short nails; clients who work with their hands; men's manicures.
Oval
Straight sides and a tip curved like the end of an egg.
Makes the fingers look longer; medium to long nails.
Pointed (almond or stiletto)
Narrow at the tip.
Fashion looks; weak and breaks easily; not for a working hand.

ul: Choose the shape with the client, from her fingers, her nail beds, her work and her wishes.
File **from each side towards the centre, in one direction**. Hold the emery board at a slight angle under the free edge and use light strokes.
Do not **saw** back and forth: it splits the layers of the nail and leaves a rough edge.
Do not file deep into the corners: it weakens the nail and can lead to splits and ingrown nails.
File natural nails **dry**, before soaking. A soaked nail is soft and tears.
Finish with the finer side of the board and check the shape from above and from the fingertip end so that all ten match.
Soak one hand in the **finger bowl** of warm, soapy water for a few minutes while you file the other. The water softens the cuticle and cleans under the nails.
Dry the hand, then apply **cuticle softener** around the base of each nail and leave it for the time the maker says.

With a wrapped orange stick or a cuticle pusher, **gently** ease the softened cuticle back off the nail plate in small circular or sweeping movements. Do not press on the matrix and do not scrape the nail plate.
Use the **nippers only on hangnails and loose, dead skin**. Cutting the living cuticle or the skin opens the way for infection and makes the cuticle grow back thicker.
Clean under the free edge with a wrapped orange stick, gently.
Wash or wipe off the softener.

blocks.note: If you nick the skin and it bleeds: put on gloves, press with clean cotton until it stops, apply an antiseptic, put the cotton in a sealed bag, clean and disinfect the tool, avoid the area, and record it. Never continue a service on a bleeding finger.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The massage relaxes the client, warms the hands, helps the blood flow and softens the skin with the cream. Use enough cream for slip, keep an even rhythm, keep one hand in contact with the client, and ask whether the pressure is comfortable.

head: Movement
How you do it
Used for
rows: Effleurage
Smooth, gliding strokes with the whole hand, from the fingers up towards the elbow.
To start and end the massage, to spread the cream, and to link the other movements.
Petrissage
Kneading: lifting, squeezing and pressing the muscles of the forearm and the palm.
Eases tension and stiffness; helps the blood flow.
Friction
Small, firm circles with the thumbs or fingertips.
Around the wrist, the finger joints and across the back of the hand.

ul: A light stretch and gentle circling of each finger joint can be added.
Do not massage over cuts, bruises, swelling, a rash, varicose veins or a recent injury, and use very light pressure on painful or arthritic joints.
Finish with effleurage, then wipe the cream off the nail plates.

blocks.p: The client sits in a comfortable chair with her feet supported on a rest or the edge of the spa, her back supported. You sit on a low stool in front of her with a straight back, not bent double over her feet. Put a towel on the floor to catch drips.

flow: Consult; check the feet, including between the toes; fill in the record card
Wash your hands; put on gloves if the Centre's rules say
Cleanse the feet
Remove old polish
Soak both feet in the spa
Dry one foot well, especially between the toes
Cut the toenails straight across and file the edges
Cuticle softener; push back the cuticles; nip loose dead skin only
Smooth hard skin with a pumice stone or foot file
Repeat for the other foot
Rinse and dry both feet
Foot and lower-leg massage
Remove cream from the nail plates
Toe separators; base coat, two coats of colour, top coat
Check, give aftercare advice, open shoes
Drain, clean and disinfect the spa; clean up and record

ul: Look at the whole foot in good light: the soles, the heels, the nails and **between the toes**, where athlete's foot hides.
Test the water with your inner wrist or elbow before the client's feet go in: warm and comfortable, not hot. A client with diabetes may not feel that the water is too hot.
Add foot soak as the maker says. Soak for a few minutes, enough to soften the skin and nails; too long makes the skin soggy and the nails tear.
**Dry the feet well, especially between the toes.** Damp skin between the toes is where fungal infections such as athlete's foot start.

Cut toenails **straight across, level with the end of the toe**, with clean clippers. Do not cut them very short and do not round the corners down into the skin: this is what causes **ingrown toenails**.
Take two or three small cuts across a wide nail rather than one big one, which can split it.
File the edge smooth in one direction, and take the sharpness off the corners without cutting into them.
Thick nails are cut after soaking, when they are softer, a little at a time.
Cuticle care is the same as for the hands: softener, a gentle push with a wrapped orange stick or pusher, nippers for loose dead skin only.

Smooth **hard skin on the heels, the balls of the feet and the sides of the big toes** with a pumice stone or foot file, in one direction, while the skin is softened. Stop when the skin feels smooth: **leave some hard skin**, because it protects the foot from pressure and rubbing.
**Never use a blade** on hard skin in a basic pedicure. A blade can cut the skin and let in infection, and in Jamaica this is work for a podiatrist.
Corns and cracked heels that bleed are referred, not treated.

Use foot cream or massage lotion. Effleurage from the toes up the foot and lower leg, petrissage of the calf and the sole, friction with the thumbs on the sole and around the ankle, then effleurage to finish.
Support the foot with one hand throughout, and keep the pressure comfortable.

**Do not massage** over cuts, swelling, bruising, varicose veins, a rash or signs of infection, and ask a client with diabetes, a heart condition or a history of blood clots to check with her doctor first.
Wipe the cream off the nail plates with remover.
Put **toe separators** between the toes so the wet polish is not smudged.
Apply base coat, two thin coats of colour and top coat, as for the hands. Tidy the edges with a wrapped orange stick.
The client wears **open-toed shoes or disposable slippers** until the polish is fully dry. Warn her before she arrives in closed shoes.

blocks.note: Many clients walk, work and play in open shoes and sandals all year, so heels get dry, dusty and cracked. Advise a daily foot cream on the heels (not between the toes) and a pumice at home once or twice a week.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: The nail plate must be **clean and free of oil and cream**, or the polish will not stick and will peel within a day. Wipe each nail with remover on a pad after the massage.
**Roll** the bottle gently between your hands to mix the polish. Do not shake it: shaking puts air bubbles into the polish, which show in the finish.
Check that the colour is the one the client agreed, in good light.

head: Coat
Why
rows: Base coat
Protects the nail plate from staining by dark colours and gives the colour something to grip.
First thin coat of colour
Thin coats dry harder and are less likely to chip or bubble than one thick coat.
Second thin coat of colour
Gives an even, full colour. Let the first coat dry a little before you apply it.
Top coat
Protects the colour from chips and scratches and adds shine.

flow: Wipe one side of the brush on the neck of the bottle
Place the brush near the base of the nail, leaving a tiny gap at the cuticle
One stroke down the centre to the free edge
One stroke down each side
Run the brush lightly along the free edge to seal it
Let it dry a little; next coat

ul: Work from the little finger towards the thumb on the hand farthest from you, so your hand does not smudge wet nails.
A small gap at the cuticle keeps the polish off the skin and stops it lifting as the nail grows.
Sealing the free edge (capping) slows chipping at the tip.
Tidy any polish on the skin with a wrapped orange stick or fine brush dipped in remover, before it dries.
If a nail **smudges** while wet, remove the polish from that nail, wipe it clean, and reapply the coats on that nail. Then check all the others.
Look at each nail in good light for smudges, bubbles, streaks, bare patches at the sides and polish on the skin, before the client leaves.
Ask the client to look too, and fix anything she is not happy with.
Let the polish harden: at least ten minutes, longer for toes, before shoes, bags, keys or handbags.

blocks.p: A client who does not want polish, for example a man or someone whose work does not allow it, has the nails smoothed and shined with a buffer instead, then cuticle oil. Buff lightly in one direction; heavy buffing thins the nail.

head: After a manicure
Why
rows: Let the polish harden fully; avoid hot water and heavy work for an hour or so.
Soft polish dents and smudges.
Wear gloves for washing up, cleaning and gardening.
Water, detergent and soil dry the skin, lift the polish and split the nails.
Use hand cream every day and cuticle oil at night.
Keeps the skin and cuticles soft and stops hangnails.
Do not use the nails as tools, and do not pick or bite the cuticles.
Causes breaks, hangnails and infection.
File a chip or rough edge in one direction with an emery board.
Stops it tearing further.
Come back in about two to four weeks.
Keeps the nails in shape.

head: After a pedicure
Why
rows: Wear open shoes until the polish is fully dry.
Closed shoes smudge wet polish.
Wash and dry the feet every day, especially between the toes.
Damp skin between the toes grows fungus.
Wear shoes that fit well and do not squeeze the toes; clean socks.
Tight shoes cause ingrown toenails, corns and hard skin.
Cut toenails straight across; do not dig at the corners.
Prevents ingrown toenails.
Foot cream on the heels, but not between the toes.
Softens hard skin without making the toe spaces damp.
See a doctor for redness, swelling, pain, a nail that changes colour, or any sore that does not heal.
These may be infections, and need medical care.

blocks.p: Suggest products that suit her, such as the hand cream or cuticle oil you used, say how to use them, and give the price in J$. Be honest and do not pressure her. Offer to book her next visit.

flow: Throw away all single-use items (emery board, orange sticks, cotton, toe separators) or give the file to the client
Any blade or sharp item into the sharps box
Clean metal tools with soap, water and a brush, then disinfect for the contact time or sterilise, dry and store closed
Drain, clean and disinfect the foot spa or bowl as the maker says; wash and disinfect the finger bowl
Towels into the laundry bin
Wipe the station, arm rest and chair with disinfectant
Close every bottle; put products away
Wipe up any water on the floor
Wash your hands
Complete the record card

blocks.p: A record card is kept for every manicure and pedicure client. It notes her health details, what was done, the products and colours used and any reaction, so the next service can be planned safely and there is a record if there is a complaint.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date and client's details
07/11/2026, Ms Latoya Grant, Mandeville
Consultation
Works as a cashier; no allergies; no diabetes; no medicines
Findings
Nails short and strong; cuticles dry; small white spot on the right index nail; no contraindications
Service
Basic manicure with polish; squoval shape
Products and colour
Cuticle softener; hand cream; base coat; coral polish; top coat
Reactions or problems
None
Advice
Gloves for washing up; hand cream daily; return in 3 weeks
Technician
K. Reid (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards hold personal and health information. Keep them private and secure, as Jamaica's data protection law requires, and show them only to staff who need them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and why cleaning comes first.
I can say which items are single-use, which are reusable and what goes in the sharps box.
I can set up a clean manicure or pedicure station.
I can name the parts of the nail and say what leuconychia, a hangnail and a callus are.
I can carry out a consultation and explain why each question matters.
I can recognise paronychia, fungal nails, athlete's foot, warts and other contraindications, and refer the client kindly.
I can explain why a client with diabetes needs extra care and how I change the service.
I can name the tools and products and say what each is for.
I can store and use nail products safely and give first aid for a splash in the eye.
I can remove polish without staining the skin.
I can describe four nail shapes and file natural nails correctly.
I can soak, soften and push back cuticles safely and use nippers only on dead skin.
I can give a hand and arm massage with effleurage, petrissage and friction, and say when not to massage.
I can give a basic pedicure, cut toenails straight across and smooth hard skin with a pumice or foot file.
I can apply base coat, two thin coats of colour and top coat, and fix a smudge.
I can give aftercare advice after a manicure and a pedicure.
I can clean up, care for the foot spa and tools, and complete a record card.

terms: A service that cleans, shapes and polishes the fingernails and cares for the hands.
The same service for the feet and toenails.
A condition or reason that means a treatment must not be carried out, or must be changed.
The hard, see-through part of the nail that is filed and painted.
The part of the nail that grows past the fingertip.
The thin layer of dead skin on the nail plate near its base, which is gently pushed back.
The living part at the base of the nail where new nail is made.
A small piece of torn skin at the side of a nail.
White spots on the nail plate, usually from a small knock.
A thick, hard patch of skin on the heel or sole formed by pressure.
An infection of the skin around a nail: red, swollen and sore.
A fungal infection of the skin, often between the toes.
A small rough growth caused by a virus; it spreads.
A toenail edge growing into the skin, often from cutting the corners down.
Removing dirt with soap and water.
Killing most germs on a cleaned tool with a chemical, for its contact time.
A machine that sterilises metal tools with steam under pressure.
Used on one client and then thrown away.
A closed, puncture-proof container for used blades and other sharp items.
A wooden stick, wrapped in cotton wool, used to push back cuticle and clean under the free edge.
A metal or rubber-tipped tool for pushing back softened cuticle.
Small cutters used only for hangnails and loose dead skin.
A product that softens dead cuticle so it can be eased off the nail.
The bowl of warm, soapy water in which the fingers soak.
The bowl or machine in which the feet soak; cleaned and disinfected after every client.
A light volcanic stone used to smooth hard skin.
Foam pieces that keep the toes apart while polish dries.
A clear coat under the colour that protects the nail and helps the polish stick.
A clear coat over the colour that protects it and adds shine.
Smooth, gliding strokes that start and end a massage.
Kneading: lifting and pressing the muscles.
Small, firm circles with the thumbs or fingertips.
The client's record of consultation, findings, service, products and any reaction.

c1.title: A nurse's hands in Brown's Town
c1.text: Nurse Carlene Watson, 44, comes to a salon in Brown's Town, St Ann, for a manicure on her day off. She washes her hands with alcohol gel many times a day at the clinic, and her hands are dry with hangnails on three fingers. She wants 'something pretty but practical'. Her nails are short; she is wearing dark red polish from two weeks ago, chipped at the tips. Trainee Abigail will do the service.

c2.title: A pedicure before a cruise in Falmouth
c2.text: Mrs Beverley Chin, 61, books a pedicure at a salon near the pier in Falmouth, Trelawny, before a cruise. She mentions that she has had diabetes for ten years and that her feet 'go numb sometimes'. When trainee Shanique looks at the feet she sees thick hard skin on both heels, with a deep crack on the left heel that is not bleeding, and an area of red, peeling skin between the fourth and fifth toes of the right foot.

c3.title: Four friends in Portmore
c3.text: Four friends arrive together at a nail studio in Portmore, St Catherine, on a Saturday afternoon for pedicures before a party. Trainee Dwayne has one foot spa and the next bowl is in use. He has one new pumice stone and one new emery board left, and the toe separators have run out. One of the friends, Kadian, has a small, hard, rough spot with black dots on the ball of her foot that hurts when she presses it.

c4.title: Polish that will not behave in Mandeville
c4.text: At the Centre's salon in Mandeville, trainee Rochelle is polishing her partner Tamara's nails after a hand massage. She shook the bottle of coral polish hard before opening it. The first coat is streaky and has tiny bubbles, and by the time she finishes the top coat the polish on two nails is already lifting at the edges. She tidies the skin with her thumbnail. Later Tamara accidentally presses her thumb against the table and smudges it.

c5.title: Closing time at a studio in Ocho Rios
c5.text: It is closing time at a nail studio in Ocho Rios, St Ann. Trainee Jodi-Ann is clearing up after the last pedicure client. She leaves the warm water in the foot spa to drain in the morning, puts the used emery board back in the drawer for tomorrow, rinses the nippers under the tap and puts them in the UV cabinet, and tops up a half-empty water bottle with polish remover to carry to the next room. A bottle of remover is standing on the windowsill in the sun.

questions.q: How should Abigail take off the chipped dark red polish?
o: Press a soaked pad on each nail for a moment, then wipe from cuticle to tip
Scrape the chipped polish off with the edge of the orange stick, then wipe
Rub each nail briskly from side to side with a pad soaked in remover
Soak the fingertips in the finger bowl first so the polish lifts off by itself
questions.why: Pressing lets the remover soften the colour, and a single wipe outwards carries it off the nail instead of into the skin. Rubbing side to side and scraping stain and scratch; water does not dissolve polish.

questions.q: Which nail shape suits Nurse Watson's wishes and her work best?
o: Long oval, to make her fingers look longer and elegant
Pointed, since it looks pretty and she asked for something pretty
Short squoval, strong and with no corners to catch on gloves
Long square, because square nails are the strongest shape
questions.why: A nurse's nails must be short, strong and snag-free, and a squoval has the strength of a square without the sharp corners. Long or pointed nails break, tear gloves and harbour germs.

questions.q: What should Abigail do about the hangnails?
o: Cut around each nail base with the nippers to remove all the cuticle
Soften, push back the cuticles, and nip only the torn pieces of skin
Leave them, because nippers are never used in a basic manicure
Pull them off with the orange stick after the hand has soaked
questions.why: Nippers are for hangnails and loose dead skin only. Cutting the living cuticle, or tearing skin away, opens the way to infection and makes the problem worse.

questions.q: Which home-care advice will do most for her dry hands?
o: Use a stronger alcohol gel so she needs to use it less often
Soak the hands in hot water each night to soften the skin
Keep the nails long so they protect the fingertips
Hand cream after every wash and cuticle oil at night
questions.why: Frequent washing and alcohol gel strip oil from the skin, which is why it dries and tears. Replacing the moisture often, and oiling the cuticles, is the practical answer; hot water and more alcohol dry it further.

questions.q: What does the red, peeling skin between Mrs Chin's toes most likely mean for the pedicure?
o: Dry skin from the sea air: carry on, with extra foot cream between the toes
Hard skin: carry on and smooth it with the pumice stone
A likely fungal infection: do not do the pedicure, and refer her
A heat rash: carry on, but keep the water a little cooler
questions.why: Red, peeling skin between the toes is the typical sign of athlete's foot, a contagious fungal infection. The feet are not soaked or treated; she is referred to a pharmacist or doctor.

questions.q: Mrs Chin says her feet go numb. Why does this matter if she does have a pedicure later?
o: She will not feel the massage, so it can be left out of the service
She may not feel hot water or a cut, and cuts may heal slowly
Numb feet mean the toenails have stopped growing and need not be cut
She will need stronger pressure than usual so that she can feel the work
questions.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet. The client cannot warn you of heat or injury, and a small wound can become badly infected, so the water is tested carefully, sharp tools stay away from the skin and the pressure is gentle.

questions.q: If her feet are clear and she comes back for the pedicure, how should the cracked heel be treated?
o: Smooth the hard skin lightly with a foot file and avoid the crack
Shave the hard skin away with a blade so the crack can close
Rub the pumice firmly into the crack until the skin is level
Soak the foot for half an hour so the crack softens and can be peeled
questions.why: Hard skin on a client with diabetes is smoothed only lightly, never with a blade, and a crack is broken skin to be avoided and, if deep, referred. Long soaks and hard rubbing damage the skin further.

questions.q: What is the best advice for Mrs Chin's feet on the cruise?
o: Walk barefoot on deck so the hard skin wears away naturally
Check her feet every day and wear shoes that fit without squeezing
Soak her feet in the ship's hot tub each evening to keep them soft
File the hard skin hard every day until the heels are smooth
questions.why: A client with diabetes should look at her feet daily for cuts and colour changes she cannot feel, and avoid tight shoes and bare feet that cause injury. Hot water and heavy filing risk burns and broken skin.

questions.q: What is the right way to handle the one foot spa for four clients?
o: Keep the same water, adding a capful of disinfectant between clients
Rinse the spa under the tap between clients and refill it
Change the water for each client and wipe the spa dry with a towel
Drain, clean and disinfect the spa, as the maker says, between clients
questions.why: Warm water carries germs from one pair of feet to the next, and a rinse or a splash of disinfectant does not make the spa safe. Each client gets a spa that has been drained, cleaned, disinfected for the contact time and refilled.

questions.q: Dwayne has one new pumice stone and one new emery board for four clients. What should he do?
o: Use them on all four, wiping them with disinfectant between clients
Get new ones for each client, or give the clients the used ones
Use them on the first client only and skip those steps for the others
Soak them in disinfectant for five minutes between each client
questions.why: Emery boards and pumice are porous and cannot be disinfected, so they are single-use. Each client needs her own, which she may keep; sharing them spreads fungal and other infections.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do about the spot on Kadian's foot?
o: File it down with the foot file so it does not hurt at the party
Avoid it, tell her privately, and suggest she gets it treated
Cover it with a plaster and give the pedicure as normal
Tell her it is a corn and cut it out carefully with the nippers
questions.why: A hard, rough spot with black dots that is painful when pressed is typical of a verruca, a wart caused by a virus that spreads. It is not touched or treated; the client is told kindly and referred.

questions.q: The toe separators have run out. What is the best plan for the polish?
o: Use twisted strips of clean paper towel between the toes
Polish the toes without separators, holding each toe apart with a finger
Apply only a base coat today and ask them to come back for colour
Use the same set of separators on all four, since they only touch the skin
questions.why: Separators keep the toes apart so wet polish is not smudged; a clean, single-use substitute does the same job. Reusing separators between clients spreads infection, and finger-holding smudges the work.

questions.q: What most likely caused the bubbles in Rochelle's first coat?
o: The coral polish was too old and had gone thick
Tamara's nails were still soft from the finger bowl
Shaking the bottle hard before opening it
The top coat was applied before the colour was dry
questions.why: Shaking beats air into the polish, and the bubbles stay in the coat on the nail. The bottle is rolled gently between the hands to mix it.

questions.q: Why is the polish lifting at the edges of two nails?
o: Massage cream was left on the nail plates before the base coat
Two coats of colour were used instead of one thick coat
The free edge was sealed, which traps air under the colour
Coral is a light colour, and light colours never stick well
questions.why: Oil or cream on the nail plate stops the polish gripping, so it peels and lifts. After a massage every nail is wiped with remover before the base coat goes on.

questions.q: How should Rochelle have tidied the polish on the skin?
o: With her thumbnail, as she did, while the polish was still wet
With a wrapped orange stick dipped in remover, before it dried
By leaving it, since polish on the skin washes off in a day or two
By wiping the whole finger with a remover-soaked pad
questions.why: A wrapped orange stick or fine brush with a little remover lifts stray polish without touching the nail. A thumbnail scratches the nail and the skin, and a soaked pad takes the colour off the nail too.

questions.q: Tamara smudges her thumb. What is the right repair?
o: Smooth the smudge over with a wet fingertip and add more top coat
Add another coat of colour on top to fill in the smudge
Remove the polish from that thumb, wipe it and reapply the coats
Take the polish off all ten nails and start the whole set again
questions.why: A smudge cannot be hidden under more polish; the nail is cleaned and the coats redone, then all the nails are checked. Only the damaged nail needs redoing.

questions.q: What should Jodi-Ann have done with the used emery board?
o: Wipe it with disinfectant and keep it for the next client
Soak it in the spa water to wash it clean overnight
Keep it in a closed drawer, because the drawer is clean
Throw it away, or give it to the client to keep
questions.why: An emery board is porous and cannot be disinfected, so it is single-use. The other steps were wrong too: water left in the spa breeds bacteria, and nippers must be cleaned and then disinfected, because a UV cabinet only stores tools that are already clean.

questions.q: Why is remover in a water bottle dangerous?
o: Plastic water bottles make the remover lose its strength
Someone could drink it, and the warnings on the label are lost
Remover must only be stored in the room where it is used
It will evaporate faster from a bottle with a narrow neck
questions.why: Products stay in their own labelled containers. A drink bottle of a clear, flammable chemical can be swallowed by mistake, and nobody can read its hazards or first aid.

questions.q: What should be done with the bottle of remover on the sunny windowsill?
o: Leave it; sunlight keeps the remover clear and fresh
Move it to a cool cupboard away from heat, with the lid tight
Keep it there but loosen the lid so pressure does not build up
Pour it into a larger bottle so the sun warms it more slowly
questions.why: Remover is flammable and gives off fumes, and heat and sunlight make both worse. It is stored cool, closed and away from heat, flames and sunlight.

questions.q: A client's toenail corner was cut down into the skin at her last visit, and it is now red and sore where it grows into the skin. What should you do?
o: Dig the corner out gently with the tip of the nippers
Cut the nail very short so the corner is well clear of the skin
Avoid the area and refer her to a doctor or podiatrist
Push the skin back from the corner with the pusher and polish as usual
questions.why: An ingrown toenail that is red and sore is a contraindication: digging or cutting makes it worse and risks infection. It is referred, and the client is advised to cut toenails straight across in future.
